entry.title: Kearney v Migration Agents Registration Authority [2026] FCA 1615
entry.content:
This was an appeal to the Federal Court from a Tribunal decision affirming cancellation of a migration agent’s registration for five years under s 303(1)(a) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal found the agent breached the Code of Conduct and was not a fit and proper person, based on nomination applications lodged for nine businesses without their knowledge or permission. Dowling J dismissed the appeal.

Key holding: Under the former reg 3(1) definition, a migration agent’s client includes any person to whom the agent agrees to provide immigration assistance, even without a retainer or the person’s express or implied acceptance.

I agree with the Authority's submissions and accept that 'client', as it was defined by reg 3(1) of the Regulations at the time of the applicant's conduct in question, includes persons to whom a registered migration agent agrees to provide immigration assistance even in the absence of a retainer or where the recipient of the assistance has not expressly or impliedly agreed to receive it.

entry.title: ZKDP and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2505
entry.content:
ZKDP sought review of a delegate’s refusal to revoke the mandatory cancellation of his visa after a 7-year-6-month drug trafficking sentence. The Tribunal found he did not pass the character test but nevertheless set aside the refusal and substituted revocation after applying Direction No. 110. It weighed community protection against ties, rehabilitation, pending charges and other factors in a fact-specific decision.

Key holding: Under s 501CA(4) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), a mandatory cancellation may be revoked where the required representations have been made and the decision-maker is satisfied that there is another reason why the original decision should be revoked.

Under s 501CA(4) of the Act, the Minister may revoke the original decision to cancel if the person makes representations in accordance with the invitation and the Minister is satisfied that the person passes the character test or there is another reason why the original decision should be revoked.

entry.title: Yang and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Citizenship) [2026] ARTA 2501
entry.content:
This was a review of a delegate’s refusal to approve Australian citizenship by descent under s 17(1A) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth), because the delegate was not satisfied the applicant had an Australian citizen parent at the time of her birth under s 16(2)(a). The Tribunal affirmed the refusal after finding the documentary evidence unreliable or insufficient and the claimed parent-child relationship with Mr Yang not established at birth.

Key holding: For the purposes of s 16(2)(a) of the Citizenship Act, a claimed parent-child relationship, whether biological or non-biological, must be shown to have existed at the time of the child’s birth and cannot be established by a later relationship.

Hence, in considering whether the Applicant may be the non-biological child of an Australian citizen parent, the relationship must have existed at the time of the birth of the child. The relationship cannot be developed at a later stage.

entry.title: Roseingrave v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1602
entry.content:
The Federal Court reviewed a Tribunal decision affirming the non-revocation of Mr Roseingrave’s visa cancellation. The Court upheld two grounds because the Tribunal treated Direction 110’s cll 8.3 and 8.4 as exhaustive and failed to evaluate his representations about the impact on his wife and son. The third ground concerning asserted Torres Strait ties failed.

Key holding: The limits of the primary considerations in Direction 110 do not relieve the Tribunal of its obligation to identify, understand and evaluate the representations made by a visa cancellation review applicant.

The correct identification of the limits of the primary considerations referred to in Direction 110 did not relieve the Tribunal of its obligation to identify, understand and evaluate the representations made by Mr Roseingrave.

entry.title: Secretary, Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure v Thaler (No 2) [2026] NSWCA 226
entry.content:
The NSW Court of Appeal dealt with a notice of motion by the Secretary seeking variations to earlier orders remitting disciplinary proceedings and costs to NCAT. The Court refused to vary the remitter because its scope was already clear, but directed NCAT under cl 29(8)(d) that it may determine the remitted costs of the appeal without being satisfied of special circumstances. It otherwise dismissed the motion, with no order as to the costs of the motion.

Key holding: The Court of Appeal may, under cl 29(8)(d) of Sch 5 to the NCAT Act, direct NCAT to determine remitted costs without requiring special circumstances under s 60.

The power extends to authorising the Tribunal to depart from the rule in s 60 (which rule is explicitly displaced in a number of places in the Act: see Schedule 3 cll 12 and 13 and Schedule 5 cll 23 and 26, and Civil and Administrative Tribunal Rules 2014, rr 38 and 38A).

entry.title: Gilbert and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS) [2026] ARTA 2484
entry.content:
Frazer Gilbert, a 21-year-old NDIS participant with epilepsy and other impairments, sought review of decisions refusing funding for air-conditioning and level 2 transport and declining to recognise his epilepsy impairments as meeting the disability requirements. The Tribunal affirmed the CEO’s decisions, finding insufficient current evidence that epilepsy formed part of a substantially reduced functional capacity and that air-conditioning was not an NDIS support. Level 1 transport funding was accepted as appropriate.

Key holding: A requested air-conditioning unit that is a standard fixture, appliance or home improvement is excluded from being an NDIS support under the Transitional Rules.

In my view, the requested air-conditioning is a standard fixture, appliance, or home improvement and is excluded by the above subitems of the Transitional Rules.

entry.title: Bhardwaj and Commissioner of Taxation (Taxation) [2026] ARTA 2482
entry.content:
The Tribunal reviewed a self-represented taxpayer’s objection decision concerning deductions for work-related car, travel, clothing, self-education, other expenses, gifts and tax affairs, plus interest on money borrowed to buy shares. It disallowed most deductions and held the interest was capital and not deductible, but allowed $67,500 as the third element of the cost base of the shares. The objection decision was varied accordingly.

Key holding: Interest under a bona fide loan is incurred in the income year it becomes due and payable and may be included in the third element of the cost base even if not paid.

The Tribunal expressed its view that, consistent with the established principle as expressed in Federal Commissioner of Taxation v James Flood Pty Ltd [1953] HCA 65; (1953) 88 CLR 492, the interest became due and payable in the 2020 - 21 income year and, accordingly, the balance of $67,500 was, if shown to be deductable or otherwise allowable in the cost base, deductible or allowable in its entirety in the 2020 - 21 income year.

entry.title: Fotu v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1589
entry.content:
The Federal Court set aside the Assistant Minister’s personal decision under s 501BA(2) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) to override an Administrative Review Tribunal decision and cancel Mr Fotu’s visa. The determinative error was the Minister’s illogical dismissal as “untenable” of the relevance of the applicant’s youth and developing maturity to the risk of reoffending. The decision was quashed on judicial review.

Key holding: Dismissing as “untenable” the evidence-supported relevance of a young offender’s developing maturity to reoffending risk is illogical or irrational and can constitute material jurisdictional error.

I do not consider a logical or rational person would have reached a conclusion that it was untenable to have regard to the applicant's maturity over time in the face of the available evidence.

entry.title: ZCGS and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2499
entry.content:
ZCGS sought merits review of a 2019 protection visa refusal under s 36(1C) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), having earlier withdrawn an AAT review of the same decision. The Tribunal held it had no jurisdiction to entertain the second application because the earlier withdrawal was taken to be a dismissal and a later application was barred. The application was dismissed under s 97 of the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024 (Cth).

Key holding: Where an applicant withdraws a merits review application and it is taken to have been dismissed, the Tribunal lacks a reviewable decision for a later application concerning the same decision.

In the Tribunal's view, the effect of the Applicant having withdrawn his first application had the effect that it was taken to have been dismissed.

entry.title: Pemberton and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS) [2026] ARTA 2481
entry.content:
This was an NDIS access review concerning a former police officer with permanent PTSD and physical impairments. The Tribunal had to decide whether his impairments caused substantially reduced functional capacity under s 24(1)(c), or whether he met the s 25 early intervention requirements. The Tribunal affirmed the reviewable decision denying access.

Key holding: An assessment of substantially reduced functional capacity under s 24(1)(c) is an objective functional assessment, so a proper functional capacity assessment carries more weight than self-report or commentary.

The functional capacity assessment conducted by Ms Sorenson carries more weight. This is because the task of assessing an applicant's functional capacity for the purposes of sections 24(1)(c) is an objective test.

entry.title: SRQY and Child Support Registrar (Social security second review) [2026] ARTA 2480

It set aside the first review decision and restored the existing 50%/50% care percentage determinations. Key holding: Where the actual care that is taking place corresponds with the existing care percentage, the care percentage determination cannot be revoked under ss 54F or 54H of the Child Support (Assessment) Act 1989.

The onus of proof in establishing fitness and propriety rests with the tax practitioner. entry.title: Testart v Testart (No 3) [2026] FCA 1558
entry.content:
This matter concerned Ms Testart’s attempt to vacate a stay and reinstate her Fair Work proceeding after the trustee of her bankrupt estate elected under s 60(2) Bankruptcy Act 1966 (Cth) to discontinue it; the sequestration order was later set aside. The Federal Court treated her application as one to set aside the discontinuance but refused relief because she did not challenge the trustee’s decision within the 60-day period in r 90-80 and gave no sufficient explanation for the delay.

Key holding: A party seeking a late procedural indulgence must satisfactorily explain the delay, and the Court will weigh prejudice and the administration of justice in deciding whether to grant it.

Accordingly, a party who seeks a late procedural indulgence must provide a satisfactory explanation for the delay, and the Court is entitled to consider not only prejudice to the opposing party but also the impact upon the administration of justice and the efficient use of judicial resources: Aon Risk Services Australia Ltd v Australian National University (2009) 239 CLR 175; UBS AG v Tyne (2018) 265 CLR 77.

entry.title: Riddell v State of Queensland (Department of Education) [2026] QIRC 338
entry.content:
The Queensland Industrial Relations Commission allowed Ms Riddell’s public service appeal against a refusal to convert her temporary HP3 Occupational Therapist employment to permanent. The Commission held the refusal was not fair and reasonable because the decision-maker confined the substantially-same-role inquiry to vacant positions, gave inadequate reasons, and treated backfilling/no vacancy as a genuine operational requirement preventing conversion.

Key holding: The absence of a vacant permanent position does not, of itself, amount to a genuine operational requirement preventing conversion of temporary employment to permanent; the decision-maker must focus on the role or a substantially same role.

As has been noted in numerous decisions from the Commission, some of which have been cited above, the lack of a vacant permanent position is not a genuine operational requirement or impediment to the Appellant's temporary employment being converted to permanent. It is expected in this scenario that a position will be created.

The Administrative Review Tribunal affirmed the reviewable decision, finding the disability and early intervention requirements were not satisfied. The case is a routine merits review of access criteria under the NDIS Act.

Key holding: For s 24(1)(c) of the NDIS Act, substantially reduced functional capacity is assessed by reference to what a person can do, not what they choose or are willing to do.

There is a distinction between a person's capacity to do a task as opposed to a person's willingness to do a task.

entry.title: BDCN and Child Support Registrar (Child support second review) [2026] ARTA 2432
entry.content:

The Father alleged the Mother ceased providing care from January 2024 when the family lost its home, with older daughters and friends said to be providing care. The Tribunal found the Mother continued to arrange and provide care, including delegated care, and affirmed the existing 100% care determination to her.

Key holding: A parent’s percentage of care is not reduced merely because care is temporarily delivered through others or because older children assist, where the parent continues to arrange, financially support and meet the children’s needs.

Taking all of the above matters into account, I am not satisfied that the care of the children actually taking place no longer corresponded with the existing percentage of care determination of 100% to the Mother for each of the 2 children.

entry.content:
This case concerned an application for Australian citizenship by descent by a New Zealand citizen with serious violent offending and non-disclosure of his criminal record. The Tribunal was not positively satisfied that he met the good character criterion and affirmed the refusal.

Key holding: For citizenship by descent under s 16(2)(c) of the Australian Citizenship Act 2007 (Cth), the Tribunal must be positively satisfied that the applicant is of good character at the time of decision; if not, the application cannot be approved.

The Tribunal notes that the good character test does not require it to form an adverse view of the Applicant's character. Rather, it must be positively persuaded or positively satisfied that the Applicant is of good character.

entry.title: Gibson and Chief Executive Officer, National Disability Insurance Agency (Practice and procedure) [2026] ARTA 2437
entry.content:
The Tribunal refused an application to appoint NDIS participant Shannon Gibson’s support coordinator, Geeta Carroll, as his litigation supporter in a Tribunal review about his NDIS plan. Although the Tribunal accepted that Mr Gibson lacked decision-making ability, it was not satisfied that the appointment was “necessary” because his representative, plan-nominee mother, interpreter, Tribunal adjustments and informal supports already allowed participation.

Key holding: Under s 67(1)(b) of the Administrative Review Tribunal Act 2024 (Cth), a litigation supporter is not “necessary” merely because appointment is desirable, expedient, convenient or preferable; it is a last-resort measure required only where available and suitable other measures do not allow the party to participate.

It follows that the use of the word necessary has the effect that an appointment that would make the proceeding easier or more convenient to manage, or that the parties would welcome, is not for that reason 'necessary'. The choice of the word emphasises that an appointment is a measure of last resort, made only where the party cannot otherwise participate.

entry.title: Baraboutis and CEO, National Disability Insurance Agency (NDIS) [2026] ARTA 2417
entry.content:

The Tribunal accepted she had physical and neurological impairments and that some were permanent, but was not satisfied they caused substantially reduced functional capacity under s 24(1)(c) of the NDIS Act. Key holding: In assessing whether impairments result in substantially reduced functional capacity under s 24(1)(c), the Tribunal must consider each specified activity as a whole rather than by reference to isolated tasks.

Further, the requirement to consider an activity as a whole, rather than by reference to tasks considered in isolation (as made plain in the amendment to s 24(1)(c)) reflects the reasoning of the Full Court of the Federal Court in National Disability Insurance Agency v Foster (2023) 295 FCR 521; [2023] FCAFC 11 ('Foster').

entry.title: Australian Securities and Investments Commission v Dawson [2026] FCA 1548
entry.content:
SXHR, a Sri Lankan unauthorised maritime arrival in immigration detention, sought judicial review of a Tribunal decision affirming refusal of a Bridging E visa under s 501(1) of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth). The Tribunal had applied Direction No 110 and refused the visa notwithstanding the applicant’s outstanding Ministerial intervention request. The Federal Court dismissed the review.

Key holding: Direction 110 requires comparison of the risk attached to refusal and grant of the visa, but not separate assessment of every possible outcome after grant where only the grant creates a risk of the applicant remaining in the community.

There is no error in that approach; nothing could have been gained by comparing the nature or extent of that risk depending on which of the two identified scenarios following the grant of a visa eventuated. DVRL does not say anything against that.

entry.title: Martin v Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (NSW) [2026] NSWSC 1288
entry.content:
This was a NSW Supreme Court appeal against Local Court convictions for a sexual act towards a child and attempted voyeurism. Hamill J allowed the appeal because the Acting Magistrate’s ex tempore reasons were inadequate and failed to address the onus and standard of proof and key exculpatory evidence and submissions. The DPP conceded error.

Key holding: A conviction will be vitiated by an error of law where the judicial officer’s reasons fail to disclose the onus and standard of proof applied and fail to explain why exculpatory evidence and submissions were rejected.

The failure to provide adequate reasons - including but not limited to, the failure to mention the requirement of proof beyond a reasonable doubt - amounted to a fundamental failure of process and amounted to a clear error of law.

entry.title: Joyce v State of Queensland (Department of the Environment, Tourism, Science and Innovation) [2026] QIRC 331

entry.title: Kulwant KAUR (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2351
entry.content:
This was a review of a refusal of a Visitor (Class FA) Subclass 600 visa on genuine temporary entrant grounds under cl 600.211. The applicant was a 59-year-old widow from India whose children all live in Australia, and the family sought to keep her onshore so she could later apply for a permanent visa. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal because it was not satisfied she genuinely intended only a temporary stay.

Key holding: The Tribunal’s task under cl 600.211 is to assess whether the applicant genuinely intends a temporary stay for the visa’s purpose, not to facilitate permanent residence.

The Tribunal does not see it as its role to facilitate the applicant's intention to remain in Australia permanently regardless of the requirements of the Visitor visa. The Tribunal's role is to simply assess whether the applicant genuinely intends to stay in Australia temporarily for the purpose for which the visa is granted.

entry.title: Triolo (Migration) [2026] ARTA 2358
entry.content:
This was a review of a delegate’s refusal to grant a 95-year-old Italian citizen a Visitor (Class FA) visa, Subclass 600. The Tribunal had to decide whether the grant would authorise a stay of more than 12 consecutive months and, if so, whether exceptional circumstances existed under cl 600.215. The Tribunal affirmed the refusal, finding no exceptional circumstances and noting other visitor-visa criteria were also in issue.

Key holding: An intention or desire to remain permanently in Australia, even if reasonable and based on need for care and medical treatment, cannot be an exceptional circumstance for a further temporary visitor visa under cl 600.215.

I also consider that, where a person clearly desires and intends to stay permanently in Australia, (however reasonable and even where it is based on an applicant's need for care and medical treatment as in this case) that desire cannot reasonably be considered to be an exceptional circumstance for the grant of a further temporary visa.
